title: Leverage cuts both ways
objectives: Compute the return on equity of a leveraged position.

screens.prose: You have £10,000.00. You borrow another £10,000.00 at 5% a year and buy £20,000.00 of shares. A year later the shares are up 10%. You sell, and repay the loan with interest.
screens.question: What return have you made on your own £10,000.00?

hints.text: Work out what the shares are worth and what you owe a year later.
Shares: £22,000.00. Loan with interest: £10,500.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the loan and its interest off the shares' value, then compare with £10,000.00.

byKey.unlev: That is the shares' return. Half of the £20,000.00 was borrowed, so your own money did better.
byKey.no-int: You doubled the shares' return but forgot the £500.00 interest on the loan.
byKey.int-all: You subtracted the 5% rate from the 10% return. The interest is paid on the borrowed half only, and the gain is on the whole position.

explain.text: The shares are worth £22,000.00 and you owe £10,500.00, leaving £11,500.00: a 15% return. You earned 10% on £20,000.00 and paid 5% on £10,000.00. Borrowing magnified the result.

screens.prose: The solid line is your return for every return on the shares, borrowing at 5%. The dashed line is buying with your own money only. Slide the leverage $L$ from 1 to 5.

derive.caption: Leverage {{L}}: asset +10% gives {{fixed((L * 0.1 - (L - 1) * r) * 100, 1)}}%, asset −10% gives {{fixed((-L * 0.1 - (L - 1) * r) * 100, 1)}}%

screens.question: As you raise $L$, what happens to the solid line?

options.text: It steepens, turning about the point where the shares earn the 5% you pay
It moves up: more return at every share return
options.why: You looked only at the right-hand side. Left of 5%, a higher leverage line sits lower: bigger losses.

options.text: It stays parallel to the dashed line
options.why: The slope is the leverage. Each 1% on the shares moves your equity $L$ per cent.
You read the slider backwards. Higher leverage makes your equity swing more, so the line steepens.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the caption's two numbers at $L = 1$ and at $L = 5$.

explain.text: At $L = 4$, a 10% rise gives 25%, but a 10% fall gives −55%. Every line passes through $(0.05, 0.05)$: when the shares earn exactly the borrowing rate, borrowing neither helps nor hurts. Above it leverage magnifies gains; below it, losses.

screens.prose: **Leverage** $L$ is the position divided by your own money, your **equity**. Your £20,000.00 of shares on £10,000.00 of equity was $L = 2$. A trader puts £50,000.00 of equity into a £150,000.00 position.
screens.question: What is the trader's leverage?

hints.text: Leverage compares the position with the equity, not with the loan.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the position by the equity.

byKey.borrowed: You divided the borrowing, £100,000.00, by the equity. Leverage uses the whole position.
byKey.inverted: You divided equity by the position. Leverage is position over equity.
byKey.loan: That is the amount borrowed. Leverage is a ratio: position over equity.

explain.text: $L = \tfrac{150{,}000}{50{,}000} = 3$, with $(L - 1) \times 50{,}000 = \text{£}100{,}000.00$ borrowed. Each 1% on the position is 3% of the trader's equity. The line on the plane is now three times as steep as the dashed one.

screens.prose: Back to $L = 2$, borrowing at 5% a year. This year the shares fall 30%.
screens.question: What is the return on your equity?

widget.placeholder: a percentage; negative for a loss
widget.label: Return on equity

hints.text: The position loses twice the shares' fall. What else do you owe?
The position loses 60% of your equity, and the interest is 5% of your equity.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double the fall, then pay the interest on the borrowed half.

byKey.no-int: You doubled the fall but forgot the interest. The loan charges 5% whatever the shares do.
byKey.unlev: That is the shares' fall. On borrowed money your equity takes twice the hit.
byKey.int-helps: You added the interest back. Interest is a cost, so it deepens the loss.

explain.text: £20,000.00 of shares falls to £14,000.00, and you owe £10,500.00. That leaves £3,500.00 of your £10,000.00: −65%. The same leverage that turned 10% into 15% turns −30% into −65%.

screens.prose: Now $L = 4$, and to keep things simple the loan charges no interest. Your equity is gone when $R_E = -1$, the dashed line.
screens.question: Drag the point along the solid line to the asset fall that wipes out your equity.

hints.text: Each 1% the asset falls costs your equity 4%.
You need $4 \times R_A = -1$.

feedback.correct: A 25% fall, $1/L$, wipes out the equity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the solid line meets the dashed line.

byKey.full: You waited for the asset to lose everything. With $L = 4$ your equity is gone long before.
byKey.three-quarters: You took $1 - 1/L$. The fall that wipes you out is $1/L$, a quarter.
byKey.P: The point is not yet where the solid line crosses $R_E = -1$.

explain.text: At $L = 4$ each 1% the asset falls costs your equity 4%, so a 25% fall costs 100%. In general a fall of $\tfrac{1}{L}$ wipes you out. At $L = 1$, unlevered, only a 100% fall does.

screens.prose: A fund holds an index at 3 times its equity, borrowing the rest at 5% a year. The index returns 8% this year. The fund's brochure says 3 times leverage turns 8% into 24%.
screens.question: What does the fund's equity actually return?

hints.text: For each £1.00 of equity, how much does the fund borrow?
It borrows £2.00 for each £1.00, and pays 5% on all of it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Triple the index return, then pay interest on the borrowing.

byKey.no-int: You tripled the index return and stopped. The fund borrowed twice its equity and pays 5% on it: 10% of equity.
byKey.int-once: You charged interest on one unit of equity. The fund borrowed two.
byKey.int-three: You charged interest on the whole position. The fund's own third is not borrowed.

explain.text: $R_E = 3 \times 0.08 - 2 \times 0.05 = 0.14$. Had the index fallen 8%, the fund would lose $0.24 + 0.10 = 0.34$ of its equity. The interest is due either way, so leverage magnifies losses more than gains.

screens.prose: Now in general. You put in equity $E$ and hold a position $L$ times as large. The position returns $R_A$, and you borrow at $r$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: The position is $LE$, so you borrow $(L - 1)E$: leverage is position over equity
At the end the position is worth $LE(1 + R_A)$ and you owe $(L - 1)E(1 + r)$: the asset's return and the loan's interest
Your equity is then $LE(1 + R_A) - (L - 1)E(1 + r)$: what is left after repaying
$R_E = L(1 + R_A) - (L - 1)(1 + r) - 1$: divide by $E$ and subtract 1
$R_E = L R_A - (L - 1) r$: the constants cancel, since $L - (L - 1) - 1 = 0$

hints.text: Start from how much you borrow.
Value everything at the end before you turn it into a return.
Borrowing, end values, equity left, divide by $E$, simplify.

feedback.correct: Borrowing, end values, equity, return, simplify.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the end-of-period equity before dividing by $E$.

byKey.d4: The return needs the end equity first: the line that subtracts the loan.
byKey.d5: The simple form comes last, after dividing by $E$.

explain.text: Check with the first screen: $L = 2$, $R_A = 0.10$, $r = 0.05$ gives $0.20 - 0.05 = 0.15$. The slope in $R_A$ is $L$, which is why the line steepens. At $L = 1$ the formula gives $R_E = R_A$: no borrowing, no effect.

screens.prose: You buy £20,000.00 of shares with £10,000.00 of your own and a £10,000.00 **margin loan** from your broker. The broker requires your equity to stay at least 25% of the position's value, its **maintenance margin**. Below that it sells your shares.
screens.question: At what position value does the broker start selling? Give two decimal places.

widget.label: Position value at the forced sale

hints.text: Your equity is the position's value minus the £10,000.00 loan.
The rule is $V - 10{,}000 \ge 0.25\,V$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write equity as $V - 10{,}000$ and set it equal to 25% of $V$.

byKey.orig: You took 25% of the original £20,000.00. The rule uses the position's value now, $V$.
byKey.zero: That is where your equity reaches zero. The broker steps in earlier, at 25%.
byKey.pct: You set the loan equal to 80% of the position. The loan is 75% of it at the trigger.

explain.text: Equity is $V - 10{,}000$, and the rule needs $V - 10{,}000 \ge 0.25V$, so $V \ge 13{,}333.33$. That is a fall of a third. Below it the broker sells, often at the worst moment, and your loss is locked in.

screens.prose: A £100,000.00 account holds £300,000.00 of shares: 3 times leverage, with £200,000.00 borrowed at 6% a year. Over three months the market falls 20%.
screens.question: By what percentage does the account's equity fall?

hints.text: Find the loss on the shares and the interest for three months.
Shares lose $0.2 \times 300{,}000$; interest is $200{,}000 \times 0.06 \times 0.25$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the share loss and three months' interest, then compare with £100,000.00.

byKey.no-int: You tripled the fall but forgot three months of interest on £200,000.00.
byKey.unlev: That is the market's fall. The account holds three times its equity.
byKey.year: You charged a whole year's interest. The period is three months.

explain.text: The shares lose $0.2 \times 300{,}000 = \text{£}60{,}000.00$ and interest costs £3,000.00, leaving £37,000.00. Volatility scales the same way: a market that swings 15% a year swings this account about 45%. A further fall of about 15% would wipe it out.

screens.prose: A hedge fund has £100m of capital. It holds £180m of shares long and £120m short. Its **gross exposure** adds the two sides; its **net exposure** subtracts the short side.
screens.question: What is the fund's gross leverage, gross exposure over capital?

hints.text: Gross exposure counts both sides as positive.
Gross is $180 + 120$ million.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the long and the short side, then divide by capital.

byKey.net: That is net leverage, $\tfrac{180 - 120}{100}$. Gross adds the two sides.
byKey.long: You counted only the long side. A short position can lose money too.
byKey.total: That is gross exposure in millions. Divide by the £100m of capital.

explain.text: Gross exposure is £300m, three times capital; net is £60m, 0.6 times. Net says which way the fund leans on the market. Gross says how much a bad day for its stock picks can cost.

ideas: Leverage $L$ is position over equity. Borrowing $(L - 1)$ times your equity multiplies every return by $L$ and charges interest on the loan.
Gains and losses scale alike, and the interest is due either way. Volatility scales with $L$ too.
A fall of $1/L$ wipes out the equity; a maintenance margin forces a sale before that.

formula.name: Return on equity
formula.note: At $L = 1$ it is $R_A$. Every line passes through $(r, r)$.

summary.trap: Leverage is not more return. It is a steeper line: bigger losses as well as gains, less the interest on the borrowing.

quiz.prose: You buy shares with your own money only, so $L = 1$. The shares return 7% in a year, and the borrowing rate is 5%.
quiz.question: What is the return on your equity?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $L = 1$ nothing is borrowed.

byKey.minus: You charged interest. At $L = 1$ you borrow nothing, so no interest is due.
byKey.plus: You added the rate. The rate matters only on borrowed money, and there is none.

explain.text: $R_E = 1 \times 0.07 - 0 \times 0.05 = 0.07$. Unlevered, your return is the asset's return.

quiz.prose: A leveraged account loses 50% of its equity in a bad year.
quiz.question: What return does it need next year to get back to where it started?

feedback.correct: Half the money must double: a 100% gain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from £100.00, lose half, and find the gain back to £100.00.

byKey.same: A 50% gain on £50.00 is only £25.00, back to £75.00. The gain is on a smaller base.
byKey.quarter: That would take £50.00 to £62.50. You need to double it.

explain.text: £100.00 falls to £50.00, and only a 100% gain returns it to £100.00. In log returns the two are symmetric: $\ln 0.5 = -0.693$ and $\ln 2 = 0.693$ (the taylor course, lesson 12). Leverage makes 50% losses far more likely.

quiz.prose: A position has $L = 2$, borrowing at 4% a year. The asset returns 12% in the year.
quiz.question: What is the return on equity?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $R_E = L R_A - (L - 1) r$.

byKey.no-int: You doubled the return and forgot the interest on the borrowed half.
byKey.double-int: You charged interest on the whole position. Only half is borrowed.
byKey.unlev: That is the asset's return. With $L = 2$ your equity moves twice as much.

explain.text: $R_E = 2 \times 0.12 - 1 \times 0.04 = 0.20$. You earn 12% on twice your money and pay 4% on the borrowed half.

quiz.question: What fall in the asset wipes out the equity?

options.why: You may have halved. With $L = 5$ each 1% on the asset is 5% on equity, so 20% is enough.
You took $1 - 1/L$. The equity is gone after a fall of $1/L$.
That is the unlevered case. Borrowed money brings the wipe-out much closer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the fall that, times 5, is 100%.

explain.text: Each 1% on the asset moves the equity 5%. A 20% fall costs $5 \times 20\% = 100\%$ of the equity.
